title: How Best To Hold Students Accountable
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin examines why many teachers hesitate to hold students accountable—citing stress, fear of resentment, past failure, and compassion for difficult home lives—and offers an attitude shift he calls the 'it's-not-me-it's-you' strategy. The idea is that misbehavior is entirely a student's choice and responsibility; the teacher's only role is to enforce the classroom management plan, which removes personal guilt or hesitation from the equation. He models the internal script teachers should adopt when enforcing a consequence, emphasizing sympathy for the disappointment without personal blame, and argues students will absorb the same mindset, separating their earned consequence from the teacher who enforces it. Linsin frames consistent, genuine accountability as an act of compassion rather than harshness, contrasting it with teachers who excuse misbehavior and inadvertently harm students' long-term chances.
points: Teachers avoid accountability due to stress, fear of resentment, past failure, and compassion for students' difficult circumstances.
The 'it's-not-me-it's-you' strategy reframes misbehavior as entirely the student's choice and responsibility, not the teacher's burden.
Enforcing a consequence should feel like simply following the agreed-upon plan, not a personal confrontation.
Students adopt the same mindset over time, mentally separating the consequence they earned from the teacher who enforces it.
Holding students accountable consistently is ultimately an act of compassion, not harshness.
quotes: Why does it pain teachers to hold students accountable? Why are some so quick to ignore misbehavior, look the other way, or make excuses for it?
The it’s-not-me-it’s-you strategy is a personal reminder that student misbehavior is not about you. It’s about them.
You are bound by your classroom management plan and therefore have but one choice when a student misbehaves: enforce a consequence.
Rest assured, holding your students accountable is an act of compassion.
Your students will adopt the same attitude. They will mentally separate the consequence (which they’ve earned of their own accord) from the enforcer (which is you).

There are scores of teachers willing to lighten the load on their students by ignoring poor behavior, looking the other way, or giving second chances. And by doing so, they are harming their chances for success.
